title: Why just-in-time sourcing doesn't kill the price argument
deck: The sharpest bear case against the framework isn't about adoption — it's about inventory. If banks source XRP three seconds before each transaction and dump it immediately after, does the price argument collapse? The answer reveals something the series left implicit.

title: The derivatives market doesn't break the model. It completes it.
deck: A reader challenged whether using spot-only volume understates XRP's settlement capacity. The answer is counterintuitive: spot-only is the correct input for settlement analysis, and a deep derivatives market is a precondition for the thesis — not a competing narrative.

title: Batch transactions on the XRPL: what they mean for the settlement thesis.
deck: The series has not addressed batch transactions on the XRPL. It should. A native protocol feature that bundles multiple atomic payments through XRP changes the liquidity demand picture — and its near-miss with a critical bug tells us something important about where the protocol is in its maturity curve.

title: Two price drivers the model doesn't capture — and why one matters more than the other.
deck: A reader argued the framework misses FASB ASC 350-60 supply depletion and HFT velocity recycling. Both deserve serious engagement. One identifies a genuine gap in the model. The other conflates two distinct kinds of velocity — and the distinction reveals something important about how the market is actually structured.

title: The price that doesn't collapse on itself.
deck: There is a calculable equilibrium band at every stage of adoption — wide enough that liquidity providers are rational to hold inventory, narrow enough that the asset isn't priced so far ahead of utility that a delay becomes a collapse. The series never formalized it. This note does.
